opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think back-testing is one of the most underrated tools we have, but you're right that it comes with a big asterisk. The basic idea is appealing: train a model on data only up to some cutoff, ask it to forecast what happened afterward, and grade it against reality. Unlike most forecasting evaluations, you don't have to wait years to find out who was right. You get a fast feedback loop, and that's incredibly valuable when you're trying to tell whether a system has real foresight or is just producing confident-sounding text.

But there are a couple of ways this can mislead you. The first is leakage. It's very hard to make sure a model trained "up to 2020" truly doesn't know anything after 2020. Information leaks through retrospectives, revised datasets, even the way people phrase things. So you can get a forecaster that looks brilliant only because it's partly remembering the answer.

The second issue is the one you're pointing at: non-stationarity. Back-testing implicitly assumes the past is a decent training ground for the future. If the world is changing faster, especially if AI is changing the dynamics themselves, then the patterns that made a forecaster good in, say, 2010 to 2020 might not be the ones that matter for 2026 to 2030. Historically, a good heuristic has been "things change more slowly than enthusiasts expect." That heuristic would back-test very well. And it might be exactly the wrong heuristic for a period of rapid transformation.

So how do I weigh it? I treat back-testing as a test of necessary, not sufficient, competence. If a forecasting system can't do well on historical periods, I don't trust it on the future. If it can, that's evidence it has absorbed something real about how institutions, markets, and technologies behave. But I'd want to supplement it in a few ways. One is to deliberately back-test on historical periods of unusually fast change, like wartime mobilization, industrialization, or the early internet, to see whether the forecaster can recognize regime shifts rather than just extrapolating trends. Another is to look at whether its reasoning is causal and mechanistic, rather than just pattern-matching on base rates, because mechanistic reasoning has a better chance of transferring when the base rates break.

And honestly, part of the value is just humility. If back-testing shows that even our best systems get blindsided by structural breaks in the past, that's an important lesson for how much confidence we should place in any forecast about a transition as unusual as the one we might be heading into.

r001.rationale: The response discusses non-stationarity and back-testing unusual periods, but does not compare future history with market prices or suggest that some aspects are less anti-inductive.

r002.rationale: The response says back-testing can inform trust in a forecasting system overall, but does not describe calibrating confidence in different components of AI forecasts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's useful but it's also kind of a trap, and I want to be careful about both halves of that.

The useful part is pretty straightforward. If you've got some forecasting method, whether it's a model or a person or a committee of people with a spreadsheet, the only way you ever get to find out if it's any good is to check it against something that actually happened. And historical data is the only thing we have that's actually happened. So back-testing is basically the minimum bar. If your method can't even retrodict the last five years of benchmark progress or compute scaling or whatever, you shouldn't trust it going forward. That's a cheap sanity check and people skip it way too often.

But the problem is that back-testing tells you how well your method would have done in a world that looked like the past. And the whole premise of a lot of what we're worried about is that the future might not look like the past. If change is accelerating, then the past is, almost by construction, the regime where your method had the easiest job. The dynamics were slower, there were fewer feedback loops, AI wasn't yet contributing meaningfully to AI research. So a method that back-tests beautifully might be exactly the kind of method that extrapolates smooth trends and then gets blindsided when something goes nonlinear.

The way I think about it is that there are really two different questions you're trying to answer. One is: is this forecasting method calibrated? And back-testing is great for that. The other is: is the underlying process I'm forecasting stationary enough that calibration transfers? And back-testing can't answer that one, basically at all. You have to make an argument from outside the data about why the mechanism driving the trend will or won't persist.

And honestly, I think the second question is where most of the real disagreement lives. When people argue about timelines, they mostly agree on what the curves looked like. They disagree about whether there's some structural reason the curve bends up or bends down, and that's a mechanistic argument, not an empirical one.

So my practical take is: do the back-testing, be honest when your method fails it, but treat a passing grade as a necessary condition rather than a sufficient one. And I'd weight it more heavily for the near term, where the world is still pretty similar to the training distribution, and much less heavily for anything past a few years out. The further out you go, the more the forecast is really just your model of the mechanism wearing a quantitative costume.

One thing I'd add is that there's a selection effect in which back-tests you see. People publish the ones that worked. If you'd done this exercise in, say, 2010 with the methods people were using then, a lot of them would have confidently told you deep learning wasn't going to do much. And the few people who got it right mostly got it right for mechanistic reasons, not because they had a better trend line.

r001.rationale: The response discusses historical back-testing and changing future dynamics, but says nothing about market prices or some future history being less anti-inductive than prices.

r002.rationale: It says back-testing is useful for assessing whether a forecasting method is calibrated, distinguishes that from whether calibration transfers to the underlying process, and gives back-tests more weight near term than farther out.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful, but there’s a limit to what it can tell you. If a forecasting method can’t predict changes we’ve already observed, using only information available beforehand, that’s a reason to be suspicious of it. But doing well on those tests doesn’t establish that it will work through a major change in the underlying process.

Acceleration itself doesn’t make forecasting impossible. You could have a trend that’s accelerating quite predictably. The harder question is whether the mechanisms driving that trend are changing—for example, if AI starts contributing substantially to AI research. Then the historical data might contain very little evidence about the feedback loop you actually care about.

So I’d use back-testing to catch mistakes and compare methods, but I wouldn’t let it justify very narrow confidence intervals. I’d also want to ask: what assumptions does this forecast depend on, and what would we expect to see if those assumptions were breaking down?

r001.rationale: The response discusses predictable acceleration and changing mechanisms, but it never compares future history with market prices or says history may be less anti-inductive.

r002.rationale: It says back-testing can catch mistakes and compare forecasting methods, while warning that success does not justify narrow confidence intervals—communicating its use in calibrating confidence across forecast components.

sol-6.1.text:
I think back-testing is useful, but it’s easy to ask more of it than it can deliver. If your forecasting method can’t make reasonable predictions about the past using only information available at the time, that’s a reason to be suspicious. But doing well on that test doesn’t establish that it will work through a major change in the underlying process.

Acceleration itself doesn’t necessarily invalidate back-testing. You could have a model that predicts acceleration, and then ask whether it would have anticipated earlier changes in pace. The harder question is whether the mechanisms driving progress are changing — for example, if AI starts substantially accelerating AI research. Historical data might give us very little evidence about that regime.

So I’d use back-testing as a check on forecasting methods, rather than as a certificate of reliability. And I’d want forecasts to make their assumptions explicit: which parts are extrapolations from observed trends, and which depend on a mechanism we haven’t really seen operate yet?

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits of historical back-testing and changing mechanisms, but says nothing about anti-induction or comparing future history with market prices.

r002.rationale: It presents back-testing as a check on forecasting methods and distinguishes trend extrapolations from untested mechanisms, but does not clearly say it calibrates confidence in different forecast components.
